text: Getting here took ten years, and it was not smooth.
The Obama Foundation picked the Jackson Park site in 2016, after choosing Chicago over rival bids from New York and Honolulu.
Then came the wait.
Because Jackson Park is an Olmsted landscape listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the project couldn't just break ground.
It needed a full federal review, the kind that weighs whether a public works project will damage a historic place.
That review ran for years.
And while it ran, a group called Protect Our Parks went to court to stop the whole thing.
They were a small group of residents, but they pushed hard.
They argued that handing public parkland to a private foundation broke the public trust that's supposed to keep parks open to everyone.
They argued the study of alternative sites was a sham, written to reach a conclusion the city had already chosen.
They argued the city had effectively given away land that belonged to all of Chicago.
They lost, again and again.
The U.S.
Supreme Court declined to take up an early appeal in 2021.
A federal judge dismissed the core suit in 2022.
The federal review itself admitted, in plain language, that the Center would alter the historic character of an Olmsted park.
The courts let it proceed anyway.
The Obamas, Governor J.B.
Pritzker, and Mayor Lori Lightfoot broke ground together on September 28, 2021.
From there it was just under five years of construction to the ribbon.
The argument the Protect Our Parks suits raised never really got answered.
It just got overruled.
